title: The Spruce Goose flies once

facts.text: On 2 November 1947, Howard Hughes lifted his giant H-4 Hercules flying boat off the water of Long Beach Harbor, California.
It was the only flight the plane ever made.
The idea came from shipbuilder Henry J. Kaiser in 1942: huge flying boats to carry troops and cargo across the ocean, safe from German U-boats.
Kaiser and Hughes signed a design contract on 16 November 1942. Kaiser dropped out in 1944, and the plane was renamed the H-4 Hercules.
Wartime limits on metal meant it was built mostly of laminated birch, so the nickname "Spruce Goose" was wrong.
Its wings were longer than a football field, and it had eight Pratt and Whitney R-4360 engines.
By 1947 the war was over, the project had cost about $23 million, and a Senate war investigating committee called Hughes to testify in August.
Hughes told the senators that if the plane was a failure, he would probably leave the country and never come back.
With copilot David Grant beside him, Hughes flew the plane low over the harbor for less than a minute, then set it back down.
Hughes never flew it again, but he kept it in a climate controlled hangar until his death in 1976.
In February 1993 it reached McMinnville, Oregon, and it is now on display at the Evergreen Aviation and Space Museum.
